transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Citrine, ML Eng), Marta Kowalska (Citrine, Infra), Ethan Chu (Citrine, CTO)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
- Deep technical discussion about continuous batching and scheduler knobs to maximize throughput while keeping tail latency under 120ms for 95th percentile on Citrine's workload.
- Focus areas: max_num_seqs, max_prefill_tokens, max_gen_tokens, context-length limits, KV cache warmup, and quantization tradeoffs.
- Action items: share config, run sustained tests, follow up on KV cache metrics.

Topics: continuous batching; scheduler tuning; max_num_seqs; token limits; KV cache behavior; quantization options; VPC/on-prem constraints; bench artifacts link

[00:00:12] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a focused deep dive on continuous batching and the scheduler knobs that matter for throughput — Priya's going to drive the config examples.

[00:00:28] Samir Patel: yea thanks, we kinda have a twitchy SLA—our app needs high qps, and when we tried a naive batcher we saw big P99 spikes. so… curious to dig in.

[00:00:44] Priya Raman: cool, quick recap: continuous batching in our runtime accumulates requests by sequence and time windows, reuses KV cache on repeated prefixes, and the main knobs you'll see are max_num_seqs, max_prefill_tokens, max_gen_tokens, and max_batch_duration_ms. also there is the scheduler priority that can preempt long sequences.

[00:01:12] Marta Kowalska: can you explain max_num_seqs again? i thought it was simply batch-size but our ops team saw different behavior.

[00:01:28] Diego Alvarez: yeah it's confusing in practice — max_num_seqs is the maximum number of active sequences the scheduler will pack into an execution slice. so if you have many short requests you can get high packing, but long prefill ones reduce available slots. it's not identical to client-side batch size.

[00:01:44] Samir Patel: got it, so if we set max_num_seqs=64 what does that imply for latency?

[00:01:56] Priya Raman: in our benchmarks, with typical 30-token generation and 128-token context prefill, 64 sequences gives best throughput but can push 95th latency up about 10–20% unless you reduce max_batch_duration_ms. there's a tradeoff: pack more sequences increases GPU utilization and tokens/sec, but adds queueing delay.

[00:02:20] Ethan Chu: does continuous batching respect customer SLOs? like can we set hard latency caps?

[00:02:28] Jordan Lee: yes, you can set latency SLOs and the scheduler has policies: strict latency-first, throughput-first, or mixed. strict latency will limit max_num_seqs and prefer shorter-prefill jobs first. mixed uses fallback models or smaller quantized variants when congestion happens.

[00:02:44] [00:03:10] Speaker 6: (inaudible)

[00:03:22] Priya Raman: practical knob recommendations for Citrine's profile (short prompts, bursty load): start with max_num_seqs=32, max_prefill_tokens=256, max_gen_tokens=64, max_batch_duration_ms=15; then raise max_num_seqs to 48 or 64 if 95th stays within SLO.

[00:03:45] Samir Patel: we tried 128 prefill once and saw KV cache thrash — any tips?

[00:03:52] Diego Alvarez: KV cache thrash usually means your session keys don't align; two things: 1) prefix caching works best when requests share common prefixes (e.g., system prompt or user history), 2) there is a cache eviction policy tied to total KV size per model instance. lowering max_prefill_tokens or enabling prefix dedup helps.

[00:04:18] Marta Kowalska: is prefix dedup automatic? does it add CPU overhead?

[00:04:28] Priya Raman: it's a best-effort heuristic — we use a short rolling hash to detect identical prefixes before sending to GPU; small CPU cost but big GPU savings if you have repeated contexts. we can toggle it per route.

[00:04:44] [00:05:02] Jordan Lee: (quick sidenote) we uploaded a micro-bench spreadsheet earlier — link in chat: https://redwood-internal.mock/benchmarks/citrine-continuous-batching-2025-04-11 — it has runs with max_num_seqs 16/32/48/64 and the token/sec numbers.

[00:05:20] Samir Patel: perfect — we'll compare to our on-prem cluster. our infra is a 4x A100-ish fleet behind a VPC NAT, shared NFS for logs. we saw weird GPU underutilization even with many inflight requests.

[00:05:36] Diego Alvarez: underutilization often from mis-sized prefill/gen balance — if prefill dominates it blocks generation steps; also check sequence padding inefficiencies when you have mixed-length requests. setting max_num_seqs to multiples of model warp size helps.

[00:05:50] Ethan Chu: model warp size? please explain.

[00:06:02] Priya Raman: it's an internal unit tied to how kernels vectorize tokens; for many models we see efficiency steps at 8/16/32 sequences. packing to those sizes reduces fragmentation.

[00:06:20] [00:07:14] Samir Patel: another problem: with quantization we lost a few hallucination tests — i think we chose int4 aggressively. talk to Diego about quantization tradeoffs.

[00:07:32] Diego Alvarez: sure — int8 tends to preserve more numeric fidelity; int4 can introduce small distributional shifts that affect sensitive tasks. our advice: run eval suite per workload. Diego: we'll give a cheat-sheet comparing int8/4-bit/ZeRO-style sharding and the perf/cost delta.

[00:07:50] Priya Raman: also note that quantized kernels interact with batching — some quantized paths are faster for large batch sizes but have higher single-request overhead, so throughput vs latency tradeoffs change.

[00:08:10] Jordan Lee: let's walk through a concrete knob table — Priya, can you read the candidate configs you recommended?

[00:08:18] Priya Raman: yep: config A (latency-first): max_num_seqs=16, max_prefill_tokens=192, max_gen_tokens=64, max_batch_duration_ms=8, scheduler_policy=latency. config B (balanced): max_num_seqs=32, prefill=256, gen=64, duration_ms=15, policy=mixed. config C (throughput): max_num_seqs=64, prefill=384, gen=128, duration_ms=30, policy=throughput + fallback to quantized variant.

[00:08:54] Marta Kowalska: when you say fallback to quantized variant, is that model-level fallback? how do you guarantee semantic consistency?

[00:09:06] Priya Raman: good Q — fallback uses compatibility profiles we test offline to ensure behavior within a tolerance window. but for strict correctness you'll want to pin to a single model; fallback is best for non-critical low-risk routes.

[00:09:22] Samir Patel: hypothetically, if we run config C in our on-prem VPC, what should we watch in cloudwatch-like metrics?

[00:09:34] Diego Alvarez: key metrics: GPU occupancy, kernel time, mean batch size, queue_wait_ms, KV_cache_hit_rate, and per-route P95/P99. Also watch for tail kernel stalls — those show as sudden drops in token/sec.

[00:09:50] [00:10:36] Speaker 2: (background noise)

[00:10:44] Jordan Lee: question from our side — what percent of your requests share a common system prompt? even a small commonality greatly helps KV reuse.

[00:10:58] Samir Patel: roughly 40% share the same system prompt + last 3 messages. others are dynamic short queries.

[00:11:12] Priya Raman: that is good — with 40% reuse you'll see KV cache lift of 20–35% tokens/sec for the prefill stage. but you need a warmup period; first 30–60 seconds of traffic will be cold.

[00:11:30] Ethan Chu: does the private deployment keep KV cache across restarts?

[00:11:38] Diego Alvarez: not across full host restarts by default — KV cache is held in GPU memory; you can snapshot and restore with a custom flow but that's advanced and will cost latency on restore. we recommend steady-state warm traffic or priming runs.

[00:11:54] Marta Kowalska: for our compliance we'll need to run in Private (VPC) — are any knobs disabled in Private vs Hosted?

[00:12:06] Jordan Lee: No major knobs disabled; Private gives you full control. only difference is some observability agents need network egress to upload aggregated metrics unless you enable on-prem retention. we can ship an offline metric collector.

[00:12:20] Samir Patel: cool. one more: token limits — we have a hard 2048 context limit in our stack, can we tune prefill to avoid dropping sessions?

[00:12:30] Priya Raman: yes, enforce max_prefill_tokens at route-level and have client-side truncation policy. also you can set max_total_tokens so the scheduler rejects requests that exceed combined prefill+gen.

[00:12:50] [00:13:18] Jordan Lee: demo time — Priya, Diego, walk them through the profiler snippets you threw in the sheet.

[00:13:22] Priya Raman: (screen share) here's a trace: 32 sequences, mixed length; you can see queue_wait spikes around 120ms when a few large prefill jobs arrive; we annotated where prefix dedup helped.

[00:13:54] Diego Alvarez: and here's the kernel timeline: prefill kernels run in parallel with generation for other slices; look at the purple bars — those are KV write/evict ops which correlate with cache churn.

[00:14:20] Samir Patel: that purple region looks like our logs — any quick remediation?

[00:14:28] Priya Raman: shorter max_prefill or enable prefix-dedup reduces churn; if you can't reduce prefix length, spread those large reqs to a separate route with its own pool.

[00:14:50] Ethan Chu: route segregation seems doable. what's the overhead of separate pools?

[00:14:58] Diego Alvarez: cost is lower utilization if traffic is imbalanced; but it gives predictable latency for the heavy route. we can suggest auto-scaling thresholds to mitigate.

[00:15:20] [00:20:00] (middle of meeting, skipped some chit-chat about hiring and product updates)

[00:20:12] Priya Raman: re: scheduler knobs file — we'll include a json snippet and a short commentary per field in the sheet.

[00:20:40] Samir Patel: for the sustained test we'll run a 2-hour window with ramp-up and 5-minute sustained peak; is there a recommended traffic pattern generator?

[00:20:56] Jordan Lee: we use gatling + a custom token-aware driver in the sheet; will share the driver and an example docker-compose for on-prem.

[00:21:20] Marta Kowalska: any gotchas with NAT egress for metric exporters?

[00:21:30] Diego Alvarez: watch TCP connection churn; prefer connection pooling and push metrics in batched intervals. we also recommend local buffering to avoid NFS write storms.

[00:21:50] Samir Patel: ok great. last technical Q: can we programmatically change max_num_seqs on the fly?

[00:21:58] Priya Raman: yes, scheduler knobs are dynamic; they can be rolled per-route with zero-downtime. changes take effect within a control-plane heartbeat (usually 5–10s).

[00:22:12] Ethan Chu: excellent.

[00:22:20] Jordan Lee: wrap-up — quick recap of what we asked you to do and what we'll deliver.

[00:22:32] Jordan Lee: Redwood deliverables: 1) tuned scheduler config + notes (Priya), 2) quantization cheat-sheet (Diego), 3) traffic generator and bench sheet link with examples (Jordan).

[00:22:48] Samir Patel: Citrine deliverables: run the 2-hour sustained test, upload logs and perf counters, and we'll meet again to iterate.

[00:23:02] Priya Raman: thanks, we'll email the artifacts and set a follow-up for the week of Apr 21.

[00:23:14] Marta Kowalska: appreciate it — helps a lot.

[00:23:20] Ethan Chu: and if we hit any compliance snag for Private we'll loop legal.

[00:23:28] Jordan Lee: perfect. end notes: shared artifacts in chat and email; next meeting pending after Citrine's run. thanks all.
